title: The Stuff You Should Know Doin’ Science Playlist: How Global Warming Works
summary: Playlist rerun of a Stuff You Should Know episode on how global warming works. The hosts distinguish global warming from climate change and weather versus climate, explain natural ice age cycles and the greenhouse effect (with a hot-car analogy), and review the main greenhouse gases: carbon dioxide, nitrous oxide, methane, and short-lived climate pollutants. They cover effects such as sea level rise (including why melting Arctic sea ice adds nothing and thermal expansion of water), more intense hurricanes, droughts, wildfires, flooding, crop losses, and ecosystem disruption. They discuss IPCC confidence language and scientific consensus, the Paris Agreement and US withdrawal, personal carbon footprint actions, and a listener mail about why reading makes you sleepy.

segments.title: Opening banter and movie show plug
segments.summary: Hosts introduce the episode and mention new movie interview episodes being dropped into the feed.

segments.title: Global warming vs climate change
segments.summary: Global warming is described as one component of broader climate change, which includes extreme weather, drought, and sea level rise.

segments.title: Weather versus climate
segments.summary: Climate is long-term average regional weather; a single snowfall or anomaly is weather, not climate change.

segments.title: Natural ice age cycles
segments.summary: Earth naturally swings between glacial and interglacial periods; a roughly five degree Celsius drop can trigger an ice age, and natural warming takes tens of thousands of years.

segments.title: IPCC and observed warming
segments.summary: The IPCC, a group of roughly 2,500 scientists, reported warming, warmer oceans, stronger westerly winds, more intense droughts, and an accelerating warming rate.

segments.title: The greenhouse effect
segments.summary: Hosts explain the greenhouse effect using a hot car analogy, then describe how atmospheric particles absorb and re-emit infrared heat, keeping Earth habitable and enabling the water cycle.

segments.title: Break
segments.summary: Short break before the discussion of greenhouse gases.

segments.title: Carbon dioxide and the carbon cycle
segments.summary: CO2 makes up a small share of the atmosphere; the natural carbon cycle is roughly balanced, but fossil fuel burning and deforestation upset it. CO2 passed 400 ppm, up about 124 ppm since preindustrial times, with fossil-fuel isotope signatures confirming human origin.

segments.title: Nitrous oxide
segments.summary: Nitrous oxide absorbs far more energy than CO2 per molecule and is released by combustion and nitrogen fertilizer; it persists for about 114 years.

segments.title: Methane and short-lived climate pollutants
segments.summary: Methane comes from coal mining, livestock, and landfills and converts to CO2; short-lived climate pollutants such as black carbon and HFCs could yield quick results if cut.

segments.title: Sea level rise and melting ice
segments.summary: Melting Arctic sea ice adds no sea level rise since it already floats, while land ice from Antarctica and Greenland does. Sea levels rose about 6.5 inches in the twentieth century and could rise up to 22 inches by 2100; water also expands as it warms.

segments.title: Impacts on humans: drought, flooding, and hurricanes
segments.summary: Warming shifts evaporation and soil moisture, causing droughts, wildfires, and severe flooding; hurricanes are becoming more intense, drawing energy from warm ocean surfaces.

segments.title: Ecosystems and salmon
segments.summary: Hosts discuss how warming disrupts interconnected ecosystems, such as coral reef decline and forests turning to grassland; salmon are given as an example of nutrient transport between ecosystems.

segments.title: Crop losses and global impact
segments.summary: Carnegie Institution estimates about five billion dollars in annual crop losses; poorer nations are hit hardest, but effects reach everyone, including Houston residents after Hurricane Harvey.

segments.title: Climate models and scientific consensus
segments.summary: IPCC computer models only matched current climate when human contributions were included. Hosts discuss the scientific consensus and how scientists use uncertainty and confidence language.

segments.title: Doubt, cost of inaction, and industry
segments.summary: Hosts discuss Peter Cigaris's 2007 cost analysis favoring mitigation, the Merchants of Doubt book, and fossil fuel companies acknowledging the issue.

segments.title: Paris Accords and US withdrawal
segments.summary: The 2014 Paris Accords had 195 countries pledge decentralized national plans to hold warming near two degrees Celsius; the US withdrew in 2017 and some cities stayed committed.

segments.title: Personal actions: carbon footprint and offsets
segments.summary: Hosts suggest reducing carbon footprint through energy use, recycling, and transport; they note hybrid and electric cars have smaller footprints and mention a future episode on carbon offsets and voting.

segments.title: Listener mail: why reading makes you sleepy
segments.summary: A chiropractor listener explains reading engages eye muscles and the nervous system in a way that dampens sympathetic response, relaxing the reader. Contact info and sign-off.
